西姆西米亞琴是埃及使用的箱式或碗式里拉琴，共鳴箱有圓形與長方形，過去埃及型多為五: The simsimiyya is a box- or bowl-shaped lyre used in Egypt, its resonator round or rectangular, once mostly five-stringed in the Egyptian type and today seen with twelve strings, the strings fixed with pegs rather than tuning rings; it is a chordophone. It has been played since ancient times, in the music of the Egyptian coast (Sawahli) and in other Egyptian genres, and it often accompanies the subagiyya musicians of Port Said, Ismailia and Suez; in Saudi Arabia and Yemen it supports traditional songs and Bedouin narrative, and it appears at festivities and on reflective occasions.
西姆西米亞琴自古即有演奏，埃及舊式琴為五弦，以弦軸固定琴弦，現代影像則可見十二弦: The simsimiyya has been played since ancient times; the old Egyptian instrument had five strings fixed with pegs, and modern images show twelve. In the nineteenth century Suez Canal workers may have brought it from the Nile valley to Egypt's northern coast, where it became an instrument of Egyptian genres such as Sawahli (coastal) music, and it appears in other Egyptian music as well. Its use spread to neighbouring countries such as Libya, Jordan and Saudi Arabia; in Saudi Arabia and Yemen it accompanies traditional songs and Bedouin narrative. In the 1980s the band El Tanbura took part in its revival, and in 2024 it was recognised by UNESCO for its role in intangible cultural heritage.
西姆西米亞琴音箱採用木質材料製作，可為圓形或矩形設計。傳統樂器的琴弦由動物腸弦或: The simsimiyya's soundbox is of wood, round or rectangular in design. On traditional instruments the strings are of animal gut or of early synthetic material, and the number of strings has grown from the traditional five to the modern twelve. The strings are fixed with tuning pegs. The frame and the supporting structure are mainly of hardwood, which keeps the instrument stable and its sound good; the whole craft reflects traditional Egyptian instrument making.
西姆西米亞琴音色明亮清脆，具有獨特的金屬質感與溫暖底蘊的結合。由於琴弦數量較少（: The simsimiyya's timbre is bright and crisp, an unusual combination of metallic quality and a warm underpinning. Because it has few strings (five traditionally, up to twelve today) its range is fairly limited, mostly from the middle register to the upper middle, and its tone carries well. The box- or bowl-shaped soundbox gives it a warm resonance and a rich set of harmonics. Beside the harp the simsimiyya is plainer and rougher; beside the pipa it is brighter. The tone it makes when plucked has an intimacy to it that suits the local character of Sawahli music on the Egyptian coast: it can set a light, lively mood, and it can also convey a deeply felt, understated musical atmosphere.
